title: Trigger recipe (v1)
description: Schema for `.tera/triggers/<name>.hcl` recipes per PRD-012 §4.3 / ADR-045 §Part 7. Mirrors `pkg/workorder/triggers.TriggerBlock` plus the file-level `version` dispatch attribute. Exactly one of the `schedule`, `topic`, `connector` and `input_adapter` variant blocks must be declared (ADR-087 D4).

name.description: Bare trigger name (the HCL block label). The loader namespaces it as <vault-id>/triggers/<name>.

worker.description: Digital-worker identity that owns Work Orders this trigger creates.

enabled.description: Tri-state stand-down switch. Unset means enabled, so a trigger authored before this attribute existed is unaffected. false keeps the recipe in the applied tree — still loaded, validated and reference-checked, so a creates naming a work-order type someone deleted is an error at tera validate rather than a surprise on the day it is re-enabled — while starting no event source, so it cannot fire. That is what it buys over the alternatives: deleting the file loses the recipe, commenting the block out rots silently because nothing parses it again, and moving it out of the applied tree makes stood-down indistinguishable from never-declared. true behaves the same as unset and is retained verbatim so tera config pull does not write an opinion the author never expressed. Time spent disabled is not missed time: on_restart_missed defaults to backfill, and re-enabling suppresses that evaluation, so re-enabling a */5 trigger that was off for a week files nothing and waits for the next real tick. The switch is trigger-level, not per-variant — it stops schedule, topic, connector and input_adapter alike.

schedule.description: Cron source. Declared as schedule { cron = ... } and takes no label, since a cron expression names no other object. Exactly one source variant must be declared (ADR-087 D4).

topic.description: Broker-topic source. The block label is the topic pattern subscribed to. Exactly one source variant must be declared (ADR-087 D4).

connector.description: Connector-event source. The block label is the connector name. Exactly one source variant must be declared (ADR-087 D4).

event.description: Event name on the connector subscription.

input_adapter.description: Input-adapter source. The block label is the adapter name. Exactly one source variant must be declared (ADR-087 D4).

predicate.description: CEL predicate evaluated against the event; the trigger fires only when it is true. Meaningful for the topic, connector and input_adapter sources; a scheduled trigger has no event to test and declaring one on it is an error.

originator.description: Declares WHO ASKED for the work a firing of this trigger files, and where the reference to resolve them by is found (ADR-132 D3). Nothing about a trigger records that today: a trigger-filed Work Order is created_by = trigger:<name>, owned by its worker, and the sender of the message that set it off survives only as whatever string an inputs entry happened to copy. PRESENCE IS THE WHOLE OF THE OPT-IN - there is no boolean beside the block, because a block carrying a required attribute already says everything an originator = true could, and a pair of switches admits a declared-and-disabled state nobody needs. reference is a CEL expression evaluated against the event, like every entry in inputs, so the author says where the reference is rather than the daemon guessing a payload field name; it is compiled when the recipe loads, against the same event environment predicate and inputs use, so a typo is an error on the recipe that contains it rather than a WARN line the night something finally fires. WHAT A REFERENCE NAMES IS NOT THIS GRAMMAR'S BUSINESS: the block says originator and reference and nothing about what is on the other end, and the resolver that reads it speaks strings in both directions. A reference the wired resolver does not recognise is a FAILED RESOLUTION - the Work Order is filed exactly as it would have been without the block (ADR-132 D2) - and not a load error, so nothing is validated about the value beyond its being a compilable expression. The block sits on the trigger rather than inside a source variant because an originator is resolved from an event and the topic, connector and input_adapter sources evaluate one identical event environment - the same placement rule and the same reason as predicate - and like predicate it is REFUSED ON A schedule TRIGGER, which has no event to resolve anything from. Declaring none is byte-for-byte today's behaviour.

reference.description: The CEL expression the originator is resolved by, evaluated against the event — in practice payload.message_id. Required: a block that resolves nothing declares nothing. It is compiled when the recipe loads, so an expression that does not compile over the event environment is refused there, naming the trigger and this attribute. Its VALUE is not validated: what a reference names is the resolver's business, and one the wired resolver does not recognise is a failed resolution at fire time rather than an error at load (ADR-132 D2).

creates.description: Work-order-type name to instantiate when the trigger fires.

inputs.description: CEL expression mapping evaluated at fire time. The compiled object becomes the new WO spec.inputs.

on_restart_missed.description: Cron-only behaviour after a daemon restart that missed ticks.

title.description: Literal title for the created Work Order.

creates_draft.description: Files the Work Order this trigger creates in the draft state instead of dispatching it (ADR-104 D1/D2): it exists, it is durable, it blocks anything that depends on it, and it does not run until somebody calls work_order.release on it. This is the trigger recipe's spelling of the draft field work_order.create already takes, and it reaches that field and nothing else - same creator, same capability, same lowering - so a drafted firing differs from an ordinary one by one bit on one create. UNSET IS BYTE-FOR-BYTE TODAY'S BEHAVIOUR, and that is a ratified default rather than a convenient one: almost no Work Order wants review before it runs, so a trigger authored before this attribute existed keeps filing live work and no existing recipe changes meaning. It is spelled creates_draft rather than draft because the bare word would sit beside enabled, the trigger's own stand-down switch, and read as a second statement about the trigger's standing; the prefix binds it to creates - what this trigger creates is a draft. The bit is trigger-level rather than per-variant, because whether filed work should be confirmed before it runs is meaningful for a schedule, a topic, a connector and an input adapter alike; PRD-021 4.4's deployment route - an unsolicited message published to a topic, matched by an existing trigger, filed for a person to confirm in the morning - is the topic case and not a restriction. It changes nothing else: the Work Order is still owned by worker, still stamped created_by = trigger:<name>, and drafting needs no grant beyond create, since a draft does not run and filing one is strictly less consequential than filing live work. The authority that matters is release, which is a separate grant and somebody else's call.
